    Personal Guidance
    Even fruit trees and weeds are interrogated — no part of creation is too humble to have witnessed Kṛṣṇa. The seeker's love refuses any hierarchy of dignity when it comes to seeking Him.
    Reflection Questions
    • Do I dismiss certain places, people, or moments as too ordinary to reveal God?
    • What humble corner of my life have I never asked to teach me about Kṛṣṇa?
    Analogy

    A row of riverside trees that have shed their fruit for travelers all summer — never tasting their own mangoes — these are the ones who know what para-artha (living for others) means. The gopīs, who have given Kṛṣṇa their everything, recognize kin in these trees and beg them: please point the way to the One we have spent ourselves on.

    Important Words
    • tapaḥ — austerity
      From √tap (to burn). In Gauḍīya theology tapas alone cannot win Kṛṣṇa — only bhakti can. Yet the gopīs imagine Earth must have done some austerity, because to a lover everything that touches the Beloved must have earned the privilege somehow. The compliment is the point.
    • keśava-aṅghri-sparśa — the touch of Lord Keśava's feet
      Compound: keśava (Kṛṣṇa) + aṅghri (foot) + sparśa (touch). Caraṇa-sparśa is the supreme grace in Vaiṣṇava devotion — Ahalyā was redeemed by it (Rāmāyaṇa), Ganges flows from it. The gopīs read Earth's bristling hairs as proof of caraṇa-sparśa just happened.
    • utpulakita — standing on end in jubilation
      From ud- + pulaka (hair standing on end). One of the eight sāttvika-vikāras (rapture-symptoms) Rūpa Gosvāmī catalogs in Bhakti-rasāmṛta-sindhu. Earth is exhibiting an aṣṭa-sāttvika sign; the gopīs read her like a devotee in trance.
    • urukrama — of Lord Vāmanadeva, who covered the universe in great steps
      Compound: uru (wide) + krama (step). The 'wide-strider' — Trivikrama-Vāmana of SB 8.18–22. The gopīs entertain that Earth's joy might date from that earlier līlā, but immediately suspect it is now — Kṛṣṇa just passed.
    • varāha — of Lord Kṛṣṇa's incarnation as a boar
      From √vrh (to lift, tear up). Varāha lifted Earth from the cosmic waters (SB 3.13). The gopīs again reach for ancient līlā to explain Earth's ecstasy, then dismiss it for the only credible explanation: He was here moments ago.
    O mother earth, what austerity did you perform to attain the touch of Lord Keśava’s lotus feet, which has brought you such great joy that your bodily hairs are standing on end? You appear very beautiful in this condition. Was it during the Lord’s current appearance that you acquired this ecstatic symptom, or was it perhaps much earlier, when He stepped upon you in His form of the dwarf Vāmanadeva, or even earlier, when He embraced you in His form of the boar Varāhadeva?
    Purport

    Śrīla Viśvanātha Cakravartī explains the thoughts of the gopīs as follows: “‘Perhaps the trees and plants [mentioned in the previous verses] did not hear our question because they were in trance, meditating on Lord Viṣṇu. Or perhaps, since they will not tell us where Kṛṣṇa has gone, they are hardhearted even though they live in a holy place. Anyway, what is the use of unnecessarily criticizing the residents of a holy place? We cannot tell if they really know where Kṛṣṇa has gone. So let us find someone who definitely knows where He is.’ Thus the gopīs concluded that since Lord Kṛṣṇa had to be somewhere on the earth, the earth herself must know His whereabouts. “Then the gopīs thought, ‘Since Kṛṣṇa always walks on the earth, she is never separated from Him and thus cannot understand how much His parents, girlfriends and servants suffer in His absence. Let us ask her what austerities she has performed to gain the great fortune of being constantly touched by the feet of Lord Keśava.’”

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    O mother earth, what austerity did you perform to attain the touch of Lord Keśava's lotus feet, which has brought you such great joy that your bodily hairs are standing on end? You appear very beautiful in this condition. Was it during the Lord's current appearance that you acquired this ecstatic symptom, or was it perhaps much earlier, when He stepped upon you in His form of the dwarf Vāmanadeva, or even earlier, when He embraced you in His form of the boar Varāhadeva?
    Commentary

    "Because they are absorbed in meditation on Visnu, they are probably not replying to us, but as residents of a holy place they are hard-hearted, since they don’t say a word to us." After this one gopis spoke, "Since we cannot tell who knows about Krsna and who does not, why do you criticize these residents of the holy place? We should ask that person who knows the truth, that person who has seen him. O friends, do you know that person?" Asking all the gopis this, that one gopi pointed at the earth with her finger. The gopis said to that sakhi, "Yes, what you say is true. Wherever Krsna is, it is somewhere on the earth. The earth is never separated from Krsna. The earth is certainly most fortunate among all the elders, girl friends, lovers, and servants, because she never knows the pain of separation. We should not ask her as we did to others previously about news of Krsna, but rather ask her what austerities she did long ago to get this good fortune. If we know that, then we also can do the same austerity and become freed from separation from Krsna." Considering in this way, they then asked, "O earth, what austerities did you perform by which you shine with bliss borne from the touch of Kesava’s feet? Because your hairs in the form of grass are standing on end, we understand that he has touched you with his feet. What austerity did you do by which you constantly are absorbed day and night in close association with Krsna. You should tell us. Hearing that, our lives will become successful" Seeing that the earth did not reply, the gopis began to consider, thinking of the past. "Your strength was shown when you bore the great burden of Vamana’s foot as he stretched his other foot from patala to svarga. By what austerity did you get that strength? (va stands for vai (certainly), or can be considered added to complete the rhythm of the verse.) Or what austerity did you do to get the firm embrace of Varaha? That austerity by which you get happiness rarely achieved by others is also joyfully performed because it brings you, a woman, into contact with a man. There is no one more fortunate than you."

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Asking about the footprints of Kṛṣṇa, they glance at the earth and then assume that the earth must have seen him since the earth is spread everywhere. They consider her sprouts of grass to be her hairs standing on end out of joy on being touched by his lotus feet. They then describe her great fortune while indicating his excellence. You must have done pious acts (tapaḥ) to touch his feet. Has the touch of his feet created your joy? Api indicates a question. Śruti says tredhā viṣṇu-vicakrame: Viṣṇu took three steps. Has your joy arisen from Trivikrama stepping with his feet to cover the three worlds, showing his power? That cannot be, since why would you show such joy now, after such a long time? Maybe it was not just touching with the foot, but Varāha lifting you up and enjoying you. Or, what was your previous act by which you attained joy in being touched Kṛṣṇa’s feet? Was it being touched by Trivikrama’s feet? Was it being embraced by Varāha? Please tell us. This indicates Kṛṣṇa’s greater glory. How can we endure separation then? You are most fortunate and we are most unfortunate. Be merciful and show us his path.

    Personal Guidance
    The gopīs envy the earth herself for receiving Kṛṣṇa's footprints. Healthy spiritual envy is not jealousy but a longing to belong as completely to God as the dust beneath His feet.
    Reflection Questions
    • Whose closeness to God do I admire — and what could I learn from their path?
    • What austerity am I willing to undertake to feel Kṛṣṇa's touch on my own life?
    Analogy

    When a king's foot brushes a particular patch of ground, that patch is forever after honored — grass grows greener there, ants build cities there, pilgrims kiss it. The gopīs see Earth's hairs standing on end and demand: what tapas did you do, Bhūmi, to deserve Govinda's foot? They are jealous of the very ground.

    Stories
    Earth as devotee — Bhūmi's appeals

    In SB 10.1, Earth-goddess Bhūmi, oppressed by the weight of asuras, took the form of a cow and approached Brahmā weeping — and her cry brought Kṛṣṇa's descent to Vraja.

    The gopīs in SB 10.30 do not know this history but speak as if they do: 'What tapas did you perform, O Earth?' Bhūmi's qualification, Gauḍīyas note, was simply her sincerity — she became the cause of His appearance, and now she carries His footprints. The gopīs honor her as a sister-devotee, even while envying her hour.

    Important Words
    • eṇa-patni — O wife of the deer
      Compound vocative: eṇa (black-buck deer) + patnī (wife). The gopīs address the doe as 'sakhī' — equal to themselves, a fellow-wife of a Beloved. Rasa-śāstra: in viraha the gopī's circle of confidantes widens to include every female creature of the forest.
    • kāntā-aṅga-saṅga — because of the physical contact with His girlfriend
      Compound: kāntā (beloved) + aṅga (limb) + saṅga (contact). The most painful word in the verse for the gopīs to utter — He was with Her, body to body. The Bhāgavatam does not soften it. Vipralambha sharpens here from absence-pain to rival-pain (mātsarya-mishrita-viraha).
    • kuca-kuṅkuma-rañjitāyāḥ — colored by the vermilion powder from her breast
      Compound: kuca (breast) + kuṅkuma (vermilion) + rañjita (dyed). The vivid evidence: He carries Her color on Him now. Rūpa Gosvāmī uses this exact image in Padyāvalī and Vidagdha-mādhava — the kuṅkuma-stain as the unconcealable proof of intimacy.
    • kunda-srajaḥ — of the garland of jasmine flowers
      Compound: kunda (white jasmine) + srajaḥ (of the garland). Kunda is the autumn-flower of Vraja, identified by the Gosvāmīs as Rādhā's preferred flower. He wears Her flower; the breeze carries Her color and Her flower at once.
    • kula-pateḥ — of the master of the group of gopīs
      Compound: kula (clan, group) + pati (lord). The gopīs name Him their collective Lord — but the irony bites: the collective Lord has just gone alone with one. Hierarchy and intimacy collide in a single epithet.
    O friend, wife of the deer, has Lord Acyuta been here with His beloved, bringing great joy to your eyes? Indeed, blowing this way is the fragrance of His garland of kunda flowers, which was smeared with the kuṅkuma from the breasts of His girlfriend when He embraced Her.
    Purport

    Śrīla Viśvanātha Cakravartī provides the following charming commentary on this verse: “The gopīs spoke to a doe, ‘O friend, wife of the deer, from the bliss in your clear eyes we can tell that Śrī Kṛṣṇa has expanded your joy with the beauty of His limbs, His face and so forth. You are eager to realize the ecstasy of seeing Kṛṣṇa, and thus your eyes are following Him. In fact, He is never lost to you.’ “Then the gopīs, seeing the doe continue to walk in her natural way, exclaimed, ‘Oh, are you telling us that you have seen Kṛṣṇa? Look! As this deer walks she constantly turns her head back to us, as if to say, “I will show Him to you; just follow me and I will show you Kṛṣṇa.” In this merciless Vṛndāvana, she is the only merciful person.’ “As the gopīs follow the doe they happen to lose sight of her, and they cry out, ‘Oh, why can’t we see the deer who is showing us the way to Kṛṣṇa?’ “One gopī suggests that Kṛṣṇa must be somewhere in the vicinity and that the deer, being afraid of Him, must have hidden herself to avoid the possible mistake of revealing His presence. Conjecturing in this way, the gopīs detect a fragrance that has by chance blown their way, and they repeatedly declare with great joy, ‘Yes! Yes! This is it! By Kṛṣṇa’s physical contact with His girlfriend, His jasmine garland was smeared with the kuṅkuma powder on Her breasts, and the fragrances of all these things are reaching us.’ Thus the gopīs smelled the aroma of the two lovers’ bodies, of Kṛṣṇa’s jasmine garland, and of the cosmetic powder on the breasts of His lover.”

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    O friend, wife of the deer, has Lord Acyuta been here with His beloved, bringing great joy to your eyes? Indeed, blowing this way is the fragrance of His garland of kunda flowers, which was smeared with the kuṅkuma from the breasts of His girlfriend when He embraced Her.
    Commentary

    Not hearing any answer the gopis thought, " Oh, why will this earth, an independent women, very proud, intoxicated with pastimes with the Lord ,whose body is marked with his symbols of flag, thunderbolt and ankusa, look upon us?" As they went forward they saw a doe and spoke to her. "O friend, wife of the buck, has Krsna come near his loved one, you (priyaya)? Though you are the wife of the buck, like us, you are dear to Krsna and Krsna is dear to you. Krsna has given you great bliss with a vision of his limbs such as face and arms. Having attained such bliss of the eyes, you follow him everywhere, and therefore Krsna is never falls from your vision (acyuta)." (drsam is plural rather the dual to show respect.) Seeing the doe go forward naturally, the gopis said, "This doe has seen Krsna. She seems to say, ‘Why should I speak, rather I will show you. Just follow behind me,’ while she moves forward and looks back at us. It seems she is the only merciful person in merciless Vrndavana." The gopis followed behind the doe, but not seeing where she had gone, then said, "Why can we no longer see the doe who was showing us where Krsna is?" In answer to this question one gopis said, "Krsna must be somewhere here. She has now become afraid of Krsna and she is hiding somewhere in order to deny that she has shown us the path." While the gopi was reasoning in this way, suddenly that gopi smelled a sweet fragrance. "Yes, yes! This is the fragrance of his body. The fragrance of his kunda flower garland tinted with the kumkuma due to contact with his beloved is spreading here." When the fragrance of their two bodies, the kumkuma and the kunda garland entered the gopis’ nostrils, they were able to verify Krsna’s whereabouts. "Though he is the enjoyer of all the gopis (kula pati) see how unjustly he has given them up and is enjoying with only one of us."

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    The following should be considered. With whom did Kṛṣṇa disappear? Later this is revealed, but now it is unclear. Śukadeva’s intention is as follows. Among all the various avatāras of the Lord I have attraction for Svayam Bhagavān Kṛṣṇa. Among all the associates of the Lord I have attraction for the people of Vraja. Among the people of Vraja I have greater attraction for the gopīs. All know this secret. Among all the gopīs I have most attraction for Rādhikā. Everyone does not know this. The greater attraction is because of the greater excellence. I hesitate to reveal her directly but I wish to reveal my heart for fear of being miserly in giving knowledge. By revealing her through the words of her friends the secret will not be apparent. By disguised words, I will reveal the truth through the speech of her rivals. If I reveal her accidently because of my absorption, I will not speak her name directly. Not just her name, I will not utter the names of the other gopīs. I will also reveal the rasas by indirect expression, not by direct statement. If someone understands the real meaning, then it will be most astonishing. Therefore first he reveals Rādhā through her friend speaking. When the Lord disappeared taking her with him, her friends had some doubt. Though they went with the others, absorbed in searching for only Kṛṣṇa, and though they were in a state of unmāda, they remained in their own group, searching for the couple, desiring his appearance at a distance. While walking around they were able to have a vision momentarily even without seeing his foot prints (verses 32.33). The friends speak this verse. The sequence of verses indicate acceptance that Rādhā was with him. Their friendship with the couple and their desire to see them is also indicated. Probably (api) Kṛṣṇa came near you with his beloved. Or api can indicate a question: O friend, did Kṛṣṇa come near you with his beloved? “Since he wanders in the forest, is it surprising that he passed by us who live here?” But he was with his beloved. “That is astonishing.” On seeing him, there will spread amazing happiness in association with her. Your eyes and the eyes of others associated with you must have experienced great bliss, because your limbs are decorated with anubhāvas indicating bliss. Seeing him with her would produce much greater bliss. You should not hide this from us. Since we are his intimate servants, we can know everything about him by the fragrance carried by the breeze. The fragrance clearly comes from a garland smeared with kuṁkuma from her breast when there was intimate association between head of the dynasty and his beloved (kānta). We perceive this because of practice. Praise for the seer, the eye and the object seen indicates the friends’ joy. The word api shows great longing and sorrow, by expressing possibility. In addressing the wife of the deer, they praise the doe’s eyes. Patnī refers to a wife who takes part in sacrifice with her husband according to patyu no yajṣa-saṁyoge. (Pāṇini 4.1.33) The deer participates in the sacrifice, and his wife is addressed as patnī. Thus the wife of the deer, the seer, is praised. Acyuta has come close (upagataḥ). This is praise for the doe’s good fortune. By mentioning the beloved there is praise for the seer (the doe) and the object seen (Kṛṣṇa and Rādhā). Their limbs took on extraordinary features when they were together. This is praise for the eye, as is the statement “Great bliss for the eye spread out.” He does not fail to be with her (acyutaḥ). This is praise for what is seen. The word vaḥ (plural) indicates not only the doe but her companions of equal stature. Thus this is praise for the seers. The garland of kunda flowers, white and beautiful by nature, is praise as the object seen. It was tinged with kuṁkuma (praise for an object seen), from association with his beloved (praise for an object seen). Kula-pateḥ indicates praise for the lover seen. Iha (here) is praise for the place receiving the fragrance. The wind, combining with the fragrance, blows everywhere. The word gandha, combining with its modifiers, indicates praise for it.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    The earth will not speak since, like Tulasī, she has the Lord’s affection and thus is a competitor, or she just does not want to speak. They then inquire from the doe, believing that she is a friend. O wife of the deer! You know about suffering in separation from a lover. Therefore please tell us. In great distress, in the distance, they see one doe. However dṛśām and vaḥ is in the plural, out of respect for her, since Kṛṣna has approached her. Or ena-patni in the singular refers to a class rather than an individual doe. Or out of many does, they ask the question to one only, who is the principal doe. Has he come here with some gopī? Did he give the greatest bliss to your eyes by showing his limbs? Otherwise you would not have such wide eyes, caused by happiness. He has given bliss greater than liberation (su-nirvṛtim). He must have revealed himself splendidly, otherwise you could not be so blissful. O friend! The doe is addressed as a friend because she has similar love of Kṛṣṇa, and she plays with the gopīs in the forest. You should not cheat us. Acyuta did not fail to distribute bliss, or he did not fail to come here. It seems they are familiar with his scent for they say that the wind is carrying his scent. It was previously said: upagīyamāna udgāyan vanitā-śata-yūthapaḥ mālāṁ bibhrad vaijayantīṁ vyacaran maṇḍayan vanam With the gopīs singing his praises, that leader of hundreds of groups of women sang loudly. He wandered in the forest wearing his Vaijayantī garland, beautifying the Vṛndāvana forest. SB 10.29.44 kaccit tulasi kalyāṇi govinda-caraṇa-priye saha tvāli-kulair bibhrad dṛṣṭas te ’ti-priyo ‘cyutaḥ O most kind Tulasī, to whom the feet of Govinda are so dear, have you seen that infallible one walk by, wearing you and encircled by swarms of bees? SB 10.30.7 Now he is wearing a jasmine garland. Thus he had three garlands. Or the vaijayantī garland was being worn and then he put on a tulasī garland when it appeared. Because the jasmine garland is beautiful in the moonlit night, he gave up the vaijayanti garland and put on the jasmine garland. Kula-pateḥ mean “of the king of Gokula, or the master of the gopīs.” Kṛṣṇa’s name is not directly mentioned out of shyness or cleverness. Having him alone as our master, we cannot maintain our lives in his absence. Therefore please quickly tell us. Or he is the master (pati) of persons who speak badly (kula). It is befitting that she is with such a person. They speak in hatred. Or he has associated with you (upagataḥ) and is still here. “Then search for him and find him.” He brought joy by his limbs. He has been seen by you, who are most fortunate. We cannot see him. “They are not here.” But the wind carries his fragrance.

    Personal Guidance
    The doe is asked because she has seen the lover. The gopīs grant other beings their own relationships with Kṛṣṇa rather than monopolizing Him. True love wants Kṛṣṇa to be loved by everyone.
    Reflection Questions
    • Do I rejoice when others love Kṛṣṇa, or do I quietly want to be the special one?
    • Whose devotion can I honor today as evidence that Kṛṣṇa is loved beyond my circle?
    Analogy

    A hunter passing through scrub leaves his scent on the leaves — a doe will smell him before she sees him. The gopīs see a doe and her mate at peace and read in the doe's calm eyes a recent gift: the breeze itself carries kuṅkuma-laced kunda-fragrance from His garland. He passed here with Her.

    Important Words
    • priyā-aṁse — on the shoulder of His beloved
      Compound: priyā (beloved-female) + aṁsa (shoulder). The most-painted moment in Vraja iconography: Kṛṣṇa's arm casually resting on Her shoulder. The gopīs note it as one would a wound — He has chosen one shoulder to lean on, and it is not theirs.
    • gṛhīta-padmaḥ — holding a lotus
      Compound: gṛhīta (held) + padma (lotus). Kṛṣṇa is twirling a lotus — the casual gesture of a lover at leisure. Padyāvalī (Rūpa Gosvāmī, attributed to multiple poets) and Vidagdha-mādhava both linger on this lotus-twirl as a signature of mādhurya.
    • rāma-anujaḥ — Kṛṣṇa, the younger brother of Balarāma
      Same compound as verse 6 — the gopīs keep naming Him by Vraja-relation, never by aiśvarya. Even in jealous distress, they cannot stop seeing Him as their playmate's little brother.
    • praṇaya-avalokaiḥ — with His love-laden glances
      Compound: praṇaya (affection of equals) + avaloka (glance). Praṇaya is a specific stage of prema in Rūpa Gosvāmī's ladder — the fifth, marked by complete trust between lovers. The trees, the gopīs imagine, have received what the gopīs themselves are now starved of.
    • ali-kulaiḥ — by the swarms of bees
      Compound: ali (bee) + kula (swarm). The bees follow Him because His tulasī-garland is in bloom and they are 'mada-andhāḥ' — blind with drunkenness. Gauḍīyas often read the bee as a figure of the bhakta intoxicated by the Lord's sweetness.
    O trees, we see that you are bowing down. When the younger brother of Rāma walked by here, followed by intoxicated bees swarming around the tulasī mañjarīs decorating His garland, did He acknowledge your obeisances with His affectionate glances? He must have been resting His arm on the shoulder of His beloved and carrying a lotus flower in His free hand.
    Purport

    The gopīs saw that the trees, bent over with abundant fruits and flowers, were offering obeisances to Lord Kṛṣṇa. The gopīs supposed Kṛṣṇa must have recently passed that way, since the trees were still bowing down. Because Śrī Kṛṣṇa had left the gopīs to go with His favorite consort, they were jealous and thus imagined that He had become fatigued from His loving affairs and was resting His left arm on the soft shoulder of His beloved. The gopīs further imagined that Kṛṣṇa must have been carrying a blue lotus in His right hand to drive away the bees eagerly trying to attack His beloved’s face after smelling its aroma. The scene was so beautiful, the gopīs imagined, that the maddened bees had left the tulasī garden to follow the two lovers.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    O trees, we see that you are bowing down. When the younger brother of Rāma walked by here, followed by intoxicated bees swarming around the tulasī maṣjarīs decorating His garland, did He acknowledge your obeisances with His affectionate glances? He must have been resting His arm on the shoulder of His beloved and carrying a lotus flower in His free hand.
    Commentary

    The gopis, discussing further clues that Krsna was right there, began to speak about the trees bending over with fruit and flowers as if bowing down to Krsna. "O trees! Did Krsna, wandering here, acknowledge or not, with an affectionate glance, your obeisance with offerings of fruit and flowers, your offspring, in your hands? But how could there an opportunity of his loving glancing upon saintly persons like you?" With envy they said, "This brother of Balarama (who is well known for his intoxicated love affairs), who must be similarly intoxicated, put his left arm on the shoulder of his weak beloved, using it as a pillow, due to fatigue after loving exchanges, and held in his right hand a blue lotus in order to fend off the bees swarming around because of the fragrance of his beloved face. Being absorbed in serving his beloved, how could he glance upon you trees? The bees have given up the tender tulasi groves and have followed behind Krsna to this place. Therefore we can understand that Krsna is hiding here somewhere. If that is so, should we follow the bees? No, it is improper for respectable persons to follow after intoxicated persons."

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Unsure when doe remained silent and staring, thinking she was stunned with great sorrow on seeing the pain of separation in the gopīs, the sakhīs left the doe and, seeing trees bowing low with fruits and flowers, thinking they were offering respects, they inquired from them. In this verse also by praising the items they attain great joy. The meaning is this. O trees! Did the brother of Balarāma take joy in your respects or not, by showing affectionate glances? They praise the qualities of the seers by indicating that the trees are the qualified objects of his mercy and affection. “Why would he not acknowledge our respects?” He was absorbed in sweet pastimes with his beloved. They knew this because of the fragrance. They were skillful at understanding their intimate pastimes. That is indicated in this verse by the description of Kṛṣṇa resting his arm on her shoulder. The general reason for not acknowledging the trees was that he was wandering around (caran) anxious for a place for his pastimes. “He always wanders around looking. What is special about today?” His arm is on the shoulder of his beloved who has great affection for him. Because her shoulder is tender he places his arm there lightly (upa). “He has come to show her to us. Why would he not acknowledge us?” He is followed by swarms of bees and he is absorbed in swinging a lotus in his right hand to prevent the bees from approaching his beloved. How can he acknowledge you? This also indicates the superb fragrance of the tulasī plants in the pastime forest. divya-gandha-tulasī-madhu-mattaiḥ ali-kulai alaghu gītām abhīṣṭam: maddened by the divine, honeylike aroma of the tulasī flowers on the garland Kṛṣṇa wears, swarms of bees sing loudly for him. (SB 10.35.10) He is followed by bees blind with intoxication from drinking the nectar. The special fragrance which arises when he presses against her body (to protect her from the bees) is shown. This indicates praise for the tulasī. The vaijayantī garland was mentioned in SB 10.29.44 and in this chapter verse 7 it is mentioned that Kṛṣṇa wears tulasī. Because it is described as most excellent, it should be inferred that he wears a tulasī garland. A garland of kunda flowers was mentioned in verse 11. It should be inferred that the vaijayantī and kunda garlands were given up because they disintegrated. By praising the various items the gopīs show their pleasure. The meaning of each word can be studied as in the previous verse. The speakers of this verse were friends of Rādhā. On the other hand the following verse is spoken by an opposing faction: tasyā amūni naḥ kṣobhaṁ kurvanty uccaiḥ padāni yat yaikāpahṛtya gopīnām raho bhunkte ‘cyutādharam These footprints of that special gopī greatly disturb us. Of all the gopīs, she alone was taken away to a secluded place, where she is enjoying the lips of Kṛṣṇa. SB 10.30.30

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Unsure when the does remained staring, thinking they were stunned with great sorrow on seeing the pain of separation in the gopīs, the sakhīs left the does and, seeing trees bowing low with fruits and flowers, thinking they were decent and offering respects, they inquired from them. Inferring that a lover had come with Kṛṣna by her fragrance previously mentioned, they now imagine the fragrance of his shoulder mixed with his arm. The fragrance of his hand was mixed with the fragrance of a lotus he was holding. This was mixed with the fragrance of her shoulder. There was also the fragrance of the tulasī on his body. Or there should be such arrangements among women lovers. He was followed by swarms of bees, blind with intoxication attracted to the sweet fragrance of the tulasī. The bees were attracted to the tulasī because the tulasī was related to Kṛṣṇa. All of this manifests a special rasa. Thinking his secret pastimes with his lover would be detected by the loud humming of the bees which were blind with intoxication, he tried walking away to get rid of them and came here, or he came here to pick the flowers from you trees. Or he came here thinking of giving mercy to you since you are plants, similar to tulasī while fulfilling his own purposes. And particularly out of affection for your offering of respects he came here. Did he accept you with affectionate glances? Those glances are very rare. Kimvā indicates a question. Please tell us. Or seeing his foot prints and, to the left, a woman’s foot prints, and seeing, to the right, the trees bowing down as if having achieved relief, they assumed he held a lotus in his right hand. Seeing groups of a woman’s footprints, deep and grouped together as if running in fear, they assumed that intoxicated bees had come. Or seeing drops of honey everywhere on the footprints, they assumed the bees had come. Or in an insane condition they uttered these words. This is mentioned in verse 14. Or since the intoxicated bees followed him, he also by contact became intoxicated. They say this in anger. Or he is followed by bees with pride (mada). It is suitable then that he is followed by us, who have lots our pride.

    Personal Guidance
    Even bowing branches become signs of Kṛṣṇa's having passed. The lover's eye reads reverence everywhere; the world is full of devotees bowing in their own way to the Lord who walked here.
    Reflection Questions
    • What in my environment today is quietly bowing toward Kṛṣṇa, if I look for it?
    • How does my own posture — inner and outer — express recognition of His presence?
    Analogy

    When royalty processes through a village, the trees bow under their flowering weight and the bees go drunk on the released perfume — and only those who saw the procession can answer whether the king nodded back. The gopīs ask the bowing trees: did the lotus-handed boy, His arm on Her shoulder, acknowledge your obeisance with His glance?

    Important Words
    • latāḥ — creepers
      The female-coded plant — the vine that clings to the tree. Rūpa Gosvāmī's Bhakti-rasāmṛta-sindhu uses latā as the canonical image for the bhakta clinging to Bhagavān's body: bhakti-latā-bīja, the seed of the creeper of devotion (CC Madhya 19).
    • kara-ja-spṛṣṭāḥ — touched by His fingernails
      Compound: kara (hand) + ja (born of, i.e. fingernails) + spṛṣṭāḥ (touched). Kara-ja-kṣata — nail-marks — is a stock erotic-rasa motif in Sanskrit kāvya. The gopīs find this evidence on the creepers and know with what relish He passed.
    • utpulakāni — joyful eruptions on the skin
      From ud- + pulaka (hair-bristling, here transferred to the creeper's bark eruptions). Same sāttvika-bhāva noun as verse 10 — the creepers, like Earth, exhibit a rapture-symptom. Vraja itself is in bhāva; only the gopīs are denied.
    • vanaspateḥ — of the tree
      Genitive of vanaspati — the 'lord of the forest' (the trunk-tree). The vine embraces the trunk as wife embraces husband; the gopīs see the marriage-image and ask the wife (vine) about Her visitor.
    Let us ask these creepers about Kṛṣṇa. Even though they are embracing the arms of their husband, this tree, they certainly must have been touched by Kṛṣṇa’s fingernails, since out of joy they are manifesting eruptions on their skin.
    Purport

    The gopīs reasoned that the creepers would not show signs of rapture merely by physical contact with their husband, a tree. Thus the gopīs concluded that although the creepers were embracing the strong limbs of their husband, they must have been touched by Lord Kṛṣṇa as He moved through the forest.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Let us ask these creepers about Kṛṣṇa. Even though they are embracing the arms of their husband, this tree, they certainly must have been touched by Kṛṣṇa's fingernails, since out of joy they are manifesting eruptions on their skin.
    Commentary

    Showing the other gopis signs that Krnsa was there, some gopi said, "O friends, ask these creepers who have signs of having the association of Krsna. You should not say that, because they are still embracing the trees, these creepers did not meet Krsna, because even while they are tightly embracing the branches of their husbands the trees, they exhibited strong desire for Krsna. They must have been touched by the nails of Krsna, for see, their hairs are standing on end. This does not take place in meeting their husbands the trees. Seeing this symptom they cannot tell us a lie, "We did not see Krsna." as the others have one after another."

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Another group of gopīs whom later ask, “Whose foot prints are these?” (SB 10.30.30) did not hear the present verses since they do not raise doubts at this time. Though some may have paid attention, they did not really hear since they did not have either attraction or hatred for Rādhā. They simply showed everyone the foot prints of Kṛṣṇa. Śukadeva in this verse shows the gopīs’ indifference to what was just said in order to show gopīs with different desires from those who just spoke. Ask this creeper embraced by the arms of her husband. “If that is so, how can you infer that they creepers associated with Kṛṣṇa?” Nūnam indicates conjecture. They have been touched by Kṛṣṇa’s fingernails. “How do you infer that?” Their hairs in the form of buds are standing on end. This is astonishing (aho). It was not like this before!

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    The trees are his devotees and follow him. They will not speak. We will ask the creepers, since they are female, like us. They say to each other, “Let us ask the creepers.” They are embracing the arms of their husbands. This is our bhāva also.

    Personal Guidance
    Creepers clinging to trees recall Kṛṣṇa's touch. The gopīs read all intimacy as a memory of His. The world's relationships become metaphors of the one Relationship they cannot stop seeking.
    Reflection Questions
    • What does the closeness I share with others teach me about my closeness with God?
    • Can I let human affection point beyond itself to the divine source it imitates?
    Analogy

    When the tide has come and gone in the night, you do not need to have seen the water — the swollen sand and the line of foam-debris suffice. The gopīs see creepers covered in goose-bumps and read the verdict: Kṛṣṇa's fingernails brushed them; the tide passed here.

    Important Words
    • unmatta-vacaḥ — speaking maddened words
      Compound: unmatta (maddened) + vacaḥ (speech). Not delirium — the Gosvāmīs name this divyonmāda, the divine madness of prema. Caitanya Mahāprabhu's biographer Kṛṣṇadāsa Kavirāja uses the same vocabulary in Caitanya-caritāmṛta Antya.
    • kṛṣṇa-anveṣaṇa — by searching for Kṛṣṇa
      Compound: kṛṣṇa + anveṣaṇa (seeking, search). This very compound names the chapter's heart-theme. Anveṣaṇa is treated in Bhakti-rasāmṛta-sindhu as one of the canonical activities of the gopī in viraha — the search itself is a limb of the rasa.
    • kātarāḥ — distraught
      From √kātar (to be pained, distressed). One of Rūpa Gosvāmī's named vyabhicārī-bhāvas (transient emotions of mahābhāva): kātarya — wounded helplessness — listed among the thirty-three intensifiers of sthāyī-bhāva.
    • anucakruḥ — they acted out
      Perfect of anu-√kṛ (to do after, imitate). The paired verb to līlāḥ in this verse — they performed the līlās. Līlā-anukaraṇa — re-enactment — becomes a recognized devotional practice in Gauḍīya tradition; the Six Gosvāmīs would re-enact Vraja-līlā in Vṛndāvana groves. The gopīs invent the practice in this verse.
    • tat-ātmikāḥ — becoming absorbed in thought of Him
      Compound: tat + ātmikāḥ. Same word as verse 2 — the chapter's refrain. Their self-identity dissolves into His identity, but as bhāva-āveśa, not Advaitin merger. They become Him while remaining themselves.
    Having spoken these words, the gopīs, distraught from searching for Kṛṣṇa, began to act out His various pastimes, fully absorbed in thoughts of Him.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Having spoken these words, the gopīs, distraught from searching for Kṛṣṇa, began to act out His various pastimes, fully absorbed in thoughts of Him.
    Commentary

    "Stunned by bliss they cannot speak," they concluded. Asking such questions to inanimate objects shows the internal love of the gopis and is a sign of unmada. Searching for Krsna while speaking in this way, the gopis could not find him. Some gopis among them gave them this advice. "By imitating the form and activities of Krsna, I will now show myself as Krsna, and this way momentarily you and I will get relief from our extreme pain." As all Krsna’s pastimes gradually came to memory, with their minds absorbed in Krsna (tad atmika) they began to enact those pastimes including the killing of Putana. Yogamaya took the form of a gopi and played the parts involving unfavorable moods in order to complete this pastime. The gopis played the favorable roles.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Speaking word like those of an insane person, the gopīs were unable to search for him because of grief (kātarāḥ). They began singing loudly as before (verse 4) and began acting out the pastimes such as killing of Pūtanā. This was because their consciousness was completely in Kṛṣṇa (tad-ātmikāḥ): they were deeply attached to him. They imitated him because of this, not because of completely non-difference with him. “She lifted her shawl above her head” (verse 20) shows effort. In saying “I am Kṛṣṇa! Just see how gracefully I move!” (verse 20) a gopī uses words to indicate that she is acting as Kṛṣṇa. They imitated the killing of Pūtanā to indicate Kṛṣṇa’s fear of her, out of deep attachment to Kṛṣṇa, just as a madman may imitate a tiger to indicate his fear of a tiger. These imitations had no elements contrary to their love for him. When one of them imitated Yaśodā, it did not represent their own type of love but was done on thinking of his infancy. Because of intense general love, they identified with Kṛṣṇa’s emotions such as fear, without touching her type of motherly love. There was no combination of conflicting bhāvas because they imitated only Kṛṣṇa’s bhāvas. This imitation was done suddenly because of their state of unmāda.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Speaking in this way (iti) the gopīs enacted Kṛṣṇa’s pastimes. Or with insane words, as was mentioned previously (unmattaka), they enacted his pastimes. The repetition of unmatta from verse 4 emphasizes their condition. Though they should not be called insane, from their questions to the various objects this is the conclusion. They imitated Kṛṣṇa’s pastimes because they were pained by separation, after searching for he who is most attractive (kṛṣṇa). Because of the pain they imitated him, not whimsically, or thinking that it would create happiness. They did this because their hearts were stolen by him (tad-ātmikāḥ). Or tad-ātmikāḥ can mean that they became absorbed in the pastimes in order to enact them. Or “by remembering him, the prāṇas of those who are pained by separation will suffer more. By the ghee of imitating the pastimes how can the ātmā remain in the hearts of those burning from the fire of increased separation?” The ātmā will not leave because it has a relationship with a sweet, soothing ocean. If they remain as they are, they will burn up. Or tad-ātmikāḥ can mean that they were absorbed in Kṛṣṇa. Their imitations depended on this. They were not whimsical.

    Atma
    Personal Guidance
    Distraught from searching, the gopīs begin re-enacting Kṛṣṇa's pastimes — when we cannot have the Lord directly, dramatizing His līlā keeps Him present. Play is a serious form of devotion.
    Reflection Questions
    • When prayer feels far away, can I tell a story of Kṛṣṇa instead?
    • What pastime of His could I quietly act out in my heart today?
    Analogy

    When a child cannot find her father at evening, she will pretend to be him — wear his slippers, take up his cane, sit in his chair — because acting him out is the closest she can get to having him. The gopīs, exhausted from searching, do exactly this: each becomes Kṛṣṇa, replays His pastimes, fills the absence with the only thing love knows how to do.

    Important Words
    • pūtanāyantyāḥ — of one who was acting like the witch Pūtanā
      Denominative participle from Pūtanā — 'behaving as Pūtanā.' The first of the chapter's līlā-anukaraṇa terms. Gauḍīyas note: the gopīs do not enact Kṛṣṇa's encounters with sages or kings — they enact the dramatic, embodied Vraja-līlās of His infancy.
    • kṛṣṇāyantī — another, who was acting like Kṛṣṇa
      Denominative participle from Kṛṣṇa — 'behaving as Kṛṣṇa.' The masculine subject becomes feminine in re-enactment; rasa-śāstra accepts this without comment. Bhāva crosses sex; what matters is the mood.
    • apibat-stanam — drank from the breast
      From √pā (to drink) + stana (breast). The exact verb-phrase of SB 10.6 where Kṛṣṇa drains Pūtanā. The gopīs are performing scripture; their bodies have absorbed the canon.
    • śakaṭā-yatīm — another who was imitating a cart
      Denominative from śakaṭa (cart). Refers to Śakaṭāsura, the cart-demon Kṛṣṇa kicked apart as an infant (SB 10.7). The gopīs play the cart, the kick, the cry — a one-verse compression of three pastimes.
    One gopī imitated Pūtanā, while another acted like infant Kṛṣṇa and pretended to suck her breast. Another gopī, crying in imitation of infant Kṛṣṇa, kicked a gopī who was taking the role of the cart demon, Śakaṭāsura.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    One gopī imitated Pūtanā, while another acted like infant Kṛṣṇa and pretended to suck her breast. Another gopī, crying in imitation of infant Kṛṣṇa, kicked a gopī who was taking the role of the cart demon, Śakaṭāsura.
    Commentary

    The imitation of Krsna’s pastimes is described in four verses. One gopi acted as Putana and another as Krsna, pretending to drink milk from her breast. One gopis cried like a baby and kicked another gopi imitating the cart.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Their imitation is described in nine verses. Situated in their own natures, they acted like Pūtanā, and did not take on her contrary mentality. One gopī acted like Kṛṣṇa (kṛṣṇāyantī). The next verse indicates that someone assumed the mood of Kṛṣṇa. (This does not mean they became Kṛṣṇa.) “Drinking milk from her breast” is only acting since acting is being discussed. One of them took the role of the cart, placing hands and feet on the ground and raising up the body.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Their imitation is described in nine verses. Anucakruḥ in the previous verse indicates that the imitation was complete. They became absorbed in the enactment. Otherwise it would have just been stated that they imitated Kṛṣṇa. One can imitate the bodily actions with one’s body, verbal actions with one’s speech and mental activities with the mind. Though one truly imitates by assuming the mood of the other person, it depends on these three elements. First three examples of bodily imitation are described. One gopī imitated Pūtanā, by using her gestures, not by dress, since that was lacking at the time. The next verses explains that one gopī thought she was Kṛṣṇa (kṛṣnārbha-bhāvavān). This was done in the confusion generated from separation. Even though not perfectly accomplished, it occurred because of the nature of pain in separation, with absorption in the pastimes. Though it is not proper for exalted devotees to imitate demons, they were overcome with special, indescribable bhāvas and thus imitated his pastimes, thinking that their friends were also overcome with such bhāvas. With intention they imitated Pūtanā and others in order to dissipate their great suffering by contact with his mind by doing that. (verse 14) Or iti means thus they were pained by searching for Kṛṣṇa. The pastimes next (anu) made all the gopīs suffering separation become full of the pastimes (tad-ātmikāḥ). Thus it was suitable that they portray demons, since demons were involved in the pastimes. They were not at fault. One gopī imitated sucking her breast, not actually sucking her breast, since it was imitation. This applies to later actions also. One imitated a cart above another gopī imitating Kṛṣṇa.

    Personal Guidance
    Imitating even Pūtanā's poisoning shows how the gopīs hold every part of Kṛṣṇa's life as precious — even the dangers He overcame. No chapter of His story is too dark to remember with love.
    Reflection Questions
    • Do I skip the difficult parts of God's story for the comforting ones?
    • What 'darker' pastime or teaching of Kṛṣṇa might I sit with today?
    Analogy

    When the master is away, the apprentices in the studio start drawing his portraits — one becomes the demon he slew, one becomes the demon's prey, one becomes the master himself raising his hand. The gopīs' Vṛndāvana becomes such a studio: Pūtanā-gopī suckling Kṛṣṇa-gopī, Śakaṭa-gopī receiving the kick, the absent līlā re-played in the empty hour.

    Stories
    Pūtanā's deliverance

    The witch Pūtanā came to poison infant Kṛṣṇa with a coated nipple. He drank the poison — and her life with it — but also, the Gosvāmīs insist, accepted her as mother because she had assumed a mother's posture (SB 10.6).

    Rūpa Gosvāmī's astonishing teaching from Bhakti-rasāmṛta-sindhu: even a malicious approach, if it takes the form of relationship, can be accepted by Kṛṣṇa as bhakti. The gopī playing Pūtanā in this verse is, in re-enactment, both the murderess and the redeemed mother — the līlā holds the paradox.

    Important Words
    • daityāyitvā — imitating a demon
      Denominative absolutive from daitya (demon, son of Diti). Refers specifically to Tṛṇāvarta. That a gopī cheerfully plays a demon in the re-enactment shows the security of Vraja: even the asuras of Kṛṣṇa's līlā are absorbed into the play.
    • kṛṣṇa-arbha — of the infant Kṛṣṇa
      Compound: kṛṣṇa + arbha (child, infant). Arbha is a rare poetic word for a very young child — emphasizing the smallness, the vulnerability that makes the demon-slaying so astonishing.
    • bhāvanām — who was assuming the mood
      Accusative of bhāvanā — mental cultivation, mood-formation. A Gauḍīya term of art: bhāvanā is the deliberate cultivation of a particular relational mood with Kṛṣṇa. The gopī playing infant Kṛṣṇa is doing bhāvanā, not pretense.
    • riṅgayām āsa — crawled about
      Periphrastic perfect of √riṅg (to crawl, of an infant). The same verb used in SB 10.8 for baby Kṛṣṇa's crawling. The gopīs' bodies are speaking scriptural Sanskrit through movement.
    • ghoṣa-niḥsvanaiḥ — with the sounding of tinkling bells
      Compound: ghoṣa (tinkling sound) + niḥsvana (sound, jingle). The ankle-bells of infant Kṛṣṇa are the sonic signature of bāla-līlā. The gopī puts them on; the absent infant returns through sound.
    One gopī took the role of Tṛṇāvarta and carried away another, who was acting like infant Kṛṣṇa, while yet another gopī crawled about, her ankle bells tinkling as she pulled her feet.
    Purport

    The gopīs started imitating all of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s pastimes, beginning from His earliest activities as a baby.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    One gopī took the role of Tṛṇāvarta and carried away another, who was acting like infant Kṛṣṇa, while yet another gopī crawled about, her ankle bells tinkling as she pulled her feet.
    Commentary

    One gopi imitated Trnavarta (daityayitva eka) who stole another gopi acting like the small child Krsna (krsnarbha bhavanam)

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    One gopī imitated the mood of Kṛṣṇa as a baby, and became absorbed in fear. One gopī crawled, making sounds with ankle bells, or employing ankle bells since she already had ankle bells on her feet. In this way she imitated Kṛṣṇa crawling about.

    Personal Guidance
    Re-enacting Tṛṇāvarta's whirlwind, the gopīs turn even demonic threats into devotional play. Threats that once terrified become beloved memories because Kṛṣṇa transformed them.
    Reflection Questions
    • What past terror in my life could I now look back on as God's protection?
    • How does my fear shrink when I remember Kṛṣṇa's track record of rescue?
    Analogy

    Children who have grown up on a single epic can re-enact any scene from memory — Tṛṇāvarta whirling, the toddler crawling with bells. The gopīs are this kind of audience: they have memorized every chapter of His bāla-līlā, and now, in His absence, they play it back through their own bodies as worship.

    Stories
    Tṛṇāvarta's whirlwind

    Sent by Kaṁsa, the whirlwind-demon Tṛṇāvarta lifted infant Kṛṣṇa into the sky — and was crushed by the same baby (SB 10.7). The gopīs of Vraja never tired of telling this story.

    Gauḍīya commentators note that Kṛṣṇa permits the demon to lift Him because He thereby gives even an asura the privilege of carrying His body. In the gopīs' enactment here, a gopī plays Tṛṇāvarta — Vraja loves even its enemies through re-play.

    Important Words
    • kṛṣṇa-rāmāyite — acting like Lord Kṛṣṇa and Lord Balarāma
      Compound denominative participle: kṛṣṇa + rāma (Balarāma) + denominative -āyita. The two brothers always paired in līlā; even a gopī cannot enact Kṛṣṇa without another gopī becoming Balarāma. Rasa demands the pair.
    • gopāyantyaḥ — acting like Their cowherd boyfriends
      Denominative participle from gopa (cowherd boy). The sakhya-rasa companions of Kṛṣṇa — Śrīdāma, Subala, etc. — are honored by the gopīs in re-enactment. Vraja loves itself across rasas: mādhurya-gopīs taste sakhya in performance.
    • vatsāyatīm — imitating the calf demon
      Denominative present participle from vatsa (calf), specifically Vatsāsura. The Bhāgavatam's vocabulary keeps generating denominatives — the gopīs are inventing rasa-grammar in real time.
    • bakāyatīm — imitating the crane demon
      Denominative from baka (crane), referring to Bakāsura. The pair Vatsa-Baka is the standard first-pair of Kṛṣṇa's pauganda demon-slayings; the gopīs are working through His résumé.
    Two gopīs acted like Rāma and Kṛṣṇa in the midst of several others, who took the role of cowherd boys. One gopī enacted Kṛṣṇa’s killing of the demon Vatsāsura, represented by another gopī, and a pair of gopīs acted out the killing of Bakāsura.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Two gopīs acted like Rāma and Kṛṣṇa in the midst of several others, who took the role of cowherd boys. One gopī enacted Kṛṣṇa's killing of the demon Vatsāsura, represented by another gopī, and a pair of gopīs acted out the killing of Bakāsura.
    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Two gopīs took the roles of Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma and others took the roles of cowherd boys to enact herding the calves. Another pastime was then enacted in the group. One gopī took the role of Kṛṣṇa and enacted the killing of Vatsāsura. One other gopīs as Kṛṣṇa enacted the killing of Bakāsura.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Two gopīs took the roles of Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma and others took the roles of cowherd boys to enact herding the calves. The word ca indicates that a gopī also imitiated Aghāsura. Present tense is used to indicate that the event was not long ago.

    Related values & verses
    Concepts
    Jiva
    Personal Guidance
    Playing Rāma and Kṛṣṇa together, the gopīs honor the brothers' bond. Spiritual life is not solo — the Lord comes with His associates, and we are invited into that family.
    Reflection Questions
    • Whom in Kṛṣṇa's circle do I most overlook, and what might that relationship teach me?
    • Who are my Balarāmas — the steady ones who walk alongside Kṛṣṇa in my life?
    Analogy

    Two children sword-fighting in a yard — one is Rāma, one is Lakṣmaṇa, the brothers of the epic. The gopīs cast themselves as Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma, others as cowherd boys, others as the calf-demon and crane-demon — Vṛndāvana becomes a stage on which the entire bāla-līlā plays simultaneously, every role taken by love.

    Stories
    Vatsāsura and Bakāsura

    Vatsāsura took the form of a calf and mixed with the herd; Kṛṣṇa caught him by the hind legs and flung him into a tree (SB 10.11). Bakāsura, the crane-demon, swallowed Kṛṣṇa and was split open from inside (SB 10.11).

    These were Kṛṣṇa's earliest demon-killings in pauganda-līlā with the cowherd boys. The gopīs re-enact them because the love-mad mind, robbed of saṁyoga, goes straight to the chapter of His childhood it most adores.

    Important Words
    • veṇum-kvaṇantīm — vibrating the flute
      Phrase: veṇu (flute) + kvaṇantī (sounding, from √kvaṇ to ring). The veṇu is Kṛṣṇa's defining instrument — Veṇu-Gopāla. The gopī mimics His flute-tone; in Gauḍīya rasa-śāstra the veṇu-nāda itself is a vibhāva (causal stimulus) of mādhurya.
    • āhūya-dūra-gāḥ — calling the far-away cows
      Phrase: āhūya (calling) + dūra (far) + gāḥ (cows). Kṛṣṇa is Go-pāla — He knows each cow by name and calls them home at dusk. The gopīs envy this naming-knowledge; in re-enactment one of them assumes it.
    • sādhu iti — 'excellent!'
      Sādhu — well done, holy, true. The same cry the demigods raise when an avatāra acts. The gopīs unconsciously perform the role of devas applauding līlā; their re-enactment is liturgically structured.
    • krīḍantīm — playing games
      Present participle of √krīḍ — the root that gives krīḍā (sport). Krīḍā is the technical Gauḍīya term for Kṛṣṇa's free, purposeless play — never duty, never necessity. The gopī plays a player; rasa is self-referential.
    When one gopī perfectly imitated how Kṛṣṇa would call the cows who had wandered far away, how He would play His flute and how He would engage in various sports, the others congratulated her with exclamations of “Well done! Well done!”
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    When one gopī perfectly imitated how Kṛṣṇa would call the cows who had wandered far away, how He would play His flute and how He would engage in various sports, the others congratulated her with exclamations of "Well done! Well done!"
    Commentary

    One gopi acted like Krsna, playing the flute to call the cows who had wandered far off, and having them follow after him.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    After enacting various pastimes, in the enacted of pastimes of the summer previous to killing Pralamba, the anubhāva called līlā is portrayed, imitating their beloved, in two verses, since this marked the appearance of his kaiśora age favorable for śṛṅgāra-rasa. Dūra-gā means cows which wandered away.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Now vocal imitation is described in five verses. Various pastimes before killing Pralamba are imitated in two verses. Since it was vocal imitation, or because of greater and greater absorption in imitating, there is no mention of imitating Kṛṣṇa. He called the cows situated far off in Vraja, just as he called the gopīs with the sound of his flute. Some praised others who had taken the role of cowherds (anuvartatīm), singing etc.

    Jiva
    Personal Guidance
    Imitating Kṛṣṇa's call to lost cows, the gopīs become the shepherd themselves. The devotee gradually inherits the work of the beloved — calling others home in His voice.
    Reflection Questions
    • Whom is Kṛṣṇa calling through me, and am I lending Him my voice?
    • What does it mean to call others home rather than just seek my own homecoming?
    Analogy

    A musician's apprentice imitates the master's flute-flourish so exactly that the audience cries out 'sādhu! sādhu!' — and the apprentice, hearing the cry, knows the master is somehow present in her playing. So with the gopī who calls the cows in Kṛṣṇa's voice; the chorus of sādhu from her sisters is the gopīs' affirmation that He has, for an instant, returned through her.

    Important Words
    • nanu-kṛṣṇaḥ-aham — indeed I am Kṛṣṇa
      The chapter's most-quoted half-line — 'verily, I am Kṛṣṇa!' Caitanya Mahāprabhu's biographers describe Him manifesting this exact mood at Purī. Gauḍīyas read it not as Advaitin aham-brahmāsmi but as the supreme symptom of viraha-āveśa, where bhāva temporarily speaks in the first person of the Beloved.
    • sva-bhujam-nyasya — placing her own arm (on a friend's shoulder)
      Phrase: sva (own) + bhuja (arm) + nyasya (placing). The very gesture verse 27 will later read in Kṛṣṇa's footprints — His arm on Her shoulder. The gopī is re-enacting the gesture they will all soon mourn discovering.
    • gatim-lalitām — my graceful movements
      Phrase: gati (gait) + lalita (graceful, charming). Lalita-tribhaṅga — the threefold-bent graceful pose — is Kṛṣṇa's iconographic standard. The gopī claims His tribhaṅga as her own walk; the parody is also an offering.
    • tat-manāḥ — with her mind fully absorbed in Him
      Compound: tat (Him) + manas (mind). Bhagavad-gītā 9.34's mat-manā bhava precept lived out by the gopīs — but in a register of intoxication rather than yogic absorption. Same lakṣaṇa, higher rasa.
    Another gopī, her mind fixed on Kṛṣṇa, walked about with her arm resting on the shoulder of a friend and declared, “I am Kṛṣṇa! Just see how gracefully I move!”
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Another gopī, her mind fixed on Kṛṣṇa, walked about with her arm resting on the shoulder of a friend and declared, "I am Kṛṣṇa! Just see how gracefully I move!"
    Commentary

    In imitating the pastimes of catching each other (cowherd boys), by the strength of the sancari bhava of unmada and the absorption in the pastimes, the gopis lost their own identity and attained a oneness with Krsna. This is described in four verses. "I am Krsna and go around with my arm on the shoulders of Subala. See my graceful actions."

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Gatiṁ refers to dance movements.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    One gopī said with certainty (nunam), “I am Kṛṣṇa.” You should not doubt this. Or O cowherds! Or O gopīs! (nunam) See my attractive movements or how I attractively walk. She was absorbed in Kṛṣṇa (tan-manāḥ). Thus there is no fault in saying this. “I am Kṛṣṇa, full of all qualities. See the gopī Lalitā, who has taken shelter of me (gatim).” Do you remember this? Kṛṣṇa had previously said this. Why is the statement not complete? Her mind was taken by Kṛṣṇa (tan-matāḥ). Or she was absorbed in the imitation.

    Walking with an arm draped on a friend's shoulder, one gopī imitates Kṛṣṇa's casual grace. Even Kṛṣṇa's ordinary gestures are worth memorizing — divinity lives in His relaxed sweetness.
    Reflection Questions
    • Which of Kṛṣṇa's small, casual qualities most attracts me?
    • How might I let one of His unhurried gestures shape my own day?

    A novice actor, finally given the lead role, walks the village street announcing 'I am the king! So the gopī, arm slung across her sister's shoulder, declares 'nanu kṛṣṇaḥ aham' — and the others believe her, because love has made it so.

    Important Words
    • mā bhaiṣṭa — don't be afraid
      The classic Vraja-shelter formula: 'do not fear.' Kṛṣṇa's standard speech to Vrajavāsīs facing demons, fire, storm. Gauḍīyas note: abhayaṁ pratiṣṭhām (BG 16.1) — fearlessness — is Bhagavān's first gift to His shelter-takers. The gopī gives the gift in His voice.
    • vāta-varṣābhyām — from wind and rain
      Dual: vāta (wind) + varṣa (rain). The specific elements of Indra's storm at Govardhana. The gopī picks the right disaster to play — she is not improvising; she is citing scripture.
    • trāṇam-vihitam-mayā — your deliverance has been arranged by me
      Phrase: trāṇa (deliverance) + vihita (arranged) + mayā (by me). The verb-phrase Kṛṣṇa uses in His own mouth when offering shelter. The gopī speaks His sentence to her sisters — for an instant, Vraja has its protector back.
    “Don’t be afraid of the wind and rain,” said one gopī. “I will save you.” And with that she lifted her shawl above her head.
    Purport

    Here a gopī enacts Lord Kṛṣṇa’s pastime of lifting Govardhana Hill.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    "Don't be afraid of the wind and rain," said one gopī. "I will save you." And with that she lifted her shawl above her head.
    Commentary

    In order graphically to depict the Govardhana pastime, one gopi with great care (yatanti) took her upper cloth and raising it above her head imitating Krsna’s lifting Govardhana.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    When wind arose they enacted the Govardhana pastime. The fire in verse 22 the pastime was not enacted because imitating intense fear would restrict śṛṅgāra-rāsa.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Absorbed imitation, she used only words, or absorbed in the pastime, she felt if the wind was actually present. This is also true of verse 22 and other enactments. This indicates that because of the separation, they had lost strength to enact with the whole body. She held her shawl high or for a long time, imitating lifting Govardhana.

    Personal Guidance
    Re-enacting the Govardhana shelter, one gopī shields others from the rain. Imitating Kṛṣṇa's protective love is itself shelter — we become safe places for others by remembering His care.
    Reflection Questions
    • For whom can I be Govardhana today — a shelter when storms come?
    • What weight am I carrying that I should lift up to Kṛṣṇa instead?
    Analogy

    A child who has heard the story of her father holding off the storm will, when the next storm comes, lift her own jacket above her playmates' heads and announce: 'I will protect you.' The gopī lifts her shawl as Kṛṣṇa lifted Govardhana — Vraja's children grow up rehearsing His shelter.

    Stories
    Govardhana lifted

    When Indra sent torrential rain to punish Vraja for honoring Govardhana hill instead of him, seven-year-old Kṛṣṇa lifted the entire hill on the little finger of His left hand and held it as an umbrella for seven days (SB 10.25). Vraja stayed dry; Indra came down to apologize.

    The gopī lifting her shawl in this verse is performing that pastime in miniature. Gauḍīyas savor that Vraja's children play 'lift Govardhana' the way other children play 'ride the horse.' Kṛṣṇa's heroism is their nursery rhyme.

      Compound vocative: duṣṭa (wicked) + ahi (snake). The very word Kṛṣṇa used to Kāliya. The gopī is reciting Kṛṣṇa's lines verbatim — her body is the stage, His script is the play.
    • daṇḍa-kṛt — the imposer of punishment
      Compound: daṇḍa (rod, punishment) + kṛt (doer). Coupled in this verse with khalānām ('on the envious'). Kṛṣṇa's avatāra-purpose paraphrased: paritrāṇāya sādhūnāṁ vināśāya ca duṣkṛtām (BG 4.8). The gopī claims His mission in the first person — the highest blasphemy if not for love.
    • ākramya-śirasi — treading upon the head
      Phrase: ākramya (treading upon, absolutive of ā-√kram) + śirasi (locative of śiras, on the head). The exact verb-noun combination Bhāgavatam uses for Kṛṣṇa stepping on Kāliya's hoods. The gopī's body is performing Bhāgavata Sanskrit.
    • nṛpa — O King
      Vocative — Śukadeva addressing Parīkṣit. The narrator surfaces here to remind us that this whole scene is being told to a dying king as the highest possible last-hearing. The frame matters: rāsa-līlā is the supreme text for the threshold of death.
    [Śukadeva Gosvāmī continued:] O King, one gopī climbed on another’s shoulders and, putting her foot on the other’s head, said, “Go away from here, O wicked snake! You should know that I have taken birth in this world just to punish the envious.”
    Purport

    Here the gopīs enact Kṛṣṇa’s chastisement of Kāliya.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    [Śukadeva Gosvāmī continued:] O King, one gopī climbed on another's shoulders and, putting her foot on the other's head, said, "Go away from here, O wicked snake! You should know that I have taken birth in this world just to punish the envious."
    Commentary

    "Dusta he" here indicates Kaliya.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Using her feet, putting them on the head of another gopī, she spoke. Nanu indicates certainty or calling out. Sometimes the word nṛpa is inserted. This indicates astonishment. Duṣṭāhe means “O wicked snake!” Leave this place or else I will punish you. Nanu means certainly. Though in the actual pastime Kṛṣṇa did not say this, the gopī said this as a conclusion or to explain the meaning of the pastime.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Nanu indicates certainty. One version has nrpa (O king)! This expresses astonishment. O Kāliya (duṣṭāhe)! Go from. Otherwise I will punish you. Using her feet, putting them on the head of another gopī, she spoke. Nanu indicates certainty or calling out. Sometimes the word nṛpa is inserted. This indicates astonishment. Duṣṭāhe means “O wicked snake!” Leave this place or else I will punish you. Nanu means certainly. Though in the actual pastime Kṛṣṇa did not say this, the gopī said this as a conclusion or to explain the meaning of the pastime.

    Personal Guidance
    One gopī climbs another's shoulders to crush Kāliya. Reenacting Kṛṣṇa's victories rehearses our trust that He has conquered every poison — past, present, and future.
    Reflection Questions
    • What 'Kāliya' in me has Kṛṣṇa already begun to subdue?
    • Can I dance on the poison instead of fearing it?
    Analogy

    When the great hero of a village kills the snake that menaced the well, every child for a year afterward dances on a coiled rope shouting 'wicked snake, away!' One gopī climbs another, plants her foot on her head, and announces her birth-purpose as Kāliya-tamer — Vraja's storytelling lives inside the bodies of its girls.

    Stories
    Kāliya subdued

    The thousand-hooded serpent Kāliya had poisoned a long reach of the Yamunā; the cows that drank fell dead. Kṛṣṇa leapt into the river, was coiled, broke free, and danced on Kāliya's hoods until the serpent submitted (SB 10.16). Kāliya's wives begged for mercy; Kṛṣṇa banished him from Yamunā but spared him.

    Gauḍīyas read Kāliya-damana as the prototype of all Kṛṣṇa-conquests of envy in the heart. The gopī here plays both the dancer and the dance — and her line 'I have taken birth to punish the envious' is Kṛṣṇa's own mission-statement repurposed.

    Important Words
    • dāva-agnim — the forest fire
      Compound: dāva (forest fire) + agni (fire). Vraja's recurring threat — three forest fires in Canto 10, all swallowed or contained by Kṛṣṇa. The element by which He proves He is also Agni's master.
    • apidadhvam — just close (your eyes)
      Imperative 2nd-pl. of api-√dhā (to cover, close). Paired with cakṣūṁṣi (eyes) — the śaraṇāgati formula in two words, Kṛṣṇa's actual instruction during the forest fire. Gauḍīyas treat this as a Vraja-form of the Bhagavad-gītā's mām ekaṁ śaraṇaṁ vraja: do not look at the fire, look at Me, by which I mean — close your eyes.
    • kṣemam — protection, well-being
      From √kṣi (to dwell safely). Kṣema and yoga are paired in Gītā 9.22 — yoga-kṣemam vahāmy aham. Kṛṣṇa Himself carries kṣema; the gopī, channeling Him, promises it in His name.
    • añjasā — with ease
      Adverb: easily, directly. The Vraja-style of Kṛṣṇa's miracles — no exertion, no display. The gopī promises rescue añjasā because she is performing His effortlessness.
    Then another gopī spoke up: My dear cowherd boys, look at this raging forest fire! Quickly close your eyes and I will easily protect you.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Then another gopī spoke up: My dear cowherd boys, look at this raging forest fire! Quickly close your eyes and I will easily protect you.
    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    One version has tatra ca: after enacting Kāliya’s punishment, then one gopīs spoke. Another version has tatraika. The word re is also seen instead of he but this is not acceptable. Kṛṣṇa ordered them to close their eyes because of the fierce fire. Since the intensity of the fire would harm the eyes, he told them to close their eyes. Though this happened in the grove of reeds, this is not mentioned. The correct form of the verb is apidhadhvam according to the rule dadhas tathośca. (Pāṇini 8.2.38) Apidadhvam is poetic license or a mistake by the transcriber. Aṣjasā means easily.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    One version has tatra ca: after enacting Kāliya’s punishment, then one gopīs spoke. This event took place there (tatra). Saving them from the forest fire also (ca) took place in the reed grove. Thus he saved the cowherds twice. Or tatra ca can mean “among the gopīs one said.” She imitated the fire in the reed grove. Anjasā means easily.

    Jiva
    Personal Guidance
    Pretending a forest fire is raging, the gopīs replay how Kṛṣṇa swallowed flames to save the cowherds. When real fires come, the heart that has rehearsed His rescues will not panic.
    Reflection Questions
    • What inner 'fire' do I keep trying to put out alone instead of asking Him to swallow?
    • How does meditating on past divine rescues steady me for present trouble?
    Analogy

    When a child has watched her father stand between her and the bonfire, she will, at any subsequent campfire, pretend to do the same for her younger siblings — small hands shielding small eyes. The gopī tells her playmate-cowherds, 'Close your eyes; I will protect you,' performing the dāvāgni-rescue Vraja still remembers in its bones.

    Stories
    The forest fire swallowed

    When a great forest fire trapped the cowherd boys and the cows on the bank of Muñjāraṇya, Kṛṣṇa told them simply to close their eyes — and when they opened them, the fire was gone (SB 10.19). He had swallowed it.

    The gopī in this verse is performing dāvāgni-grāsa. Gauḍīyas note: the close-your-eyes-and-trust formula is the most condensed śaraṇāgati in all of Canto 10. The pastime fits into one verse; the lesson fits into two words: cakṣūṁṣi apidadhvam — close your eyes.

    Important Words
    • ulūkhale-badhnāmi — I am binding to the grinding mortar
      Phrase: ulūkhala (mortar) + badhnāmi (I bind). Yaśodā's exact action of SB 10.9. Dāma-bandhana is the supreme proof in Gauḍīya theology that love-rope alone holds Bhagavān; the gopī here speaks Yaśodā's verb in the first person.
    • bhāṇḍa-bhettāram — the breaker of pots
      Compound: bhāṇḍa (pot) + bhettṛ (breaker, from √bhid). Kṛṣṇa's signature offense in Vraja — breaking the gopīs' yogurt-pots to steal butter. The gopīs love Him for this crime; in re-enactment they recite it like a litany.
    • haiyam-gava-muṣam — the stealer of the freshly-churned butter
      Compound: haiyaṅgavīna (fresh butter, from hyas-go-pīna 'yesterday's cow-milk') + muṣ (thief). The technical word for the previous day's butter — the most-prized prize. Kṛṣṇa is mākhana-cora, the butter-thief; this verse names His sacred crime.
    • bhīti-viḍambanam — the pretense of fear
      Compound: bhīti (fear) + viḍambana (mockery, imitation). The fear is not real — Kṛṣṇa in Vraja is never genuinely afraid. The Gauḍīya teaching: even His seeming-fear before Yaśodā is rasa-display, not weakness. The gopī enacts this with bhakta precision.
    One gopī tied up her slender companion with a flower garland and said, “Now I will bind this boy who has broken the butter pots and stolen the butter.” The second gopī then covered her face and beautiful eyes, pretending to be afraid.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    One gopī tied up her slender companion with a flower garland and said, "Now I will bind this boy who has broken the butter pots and stolen the butter." The second gopī then covered her face and beautiful eyes, pretending to be afraid.
    Commentary

    When the sudden appearance of strong unmada was pacified, the identification with Krsna also slackened. Returning to their identities as gopis, seeing one gopi showing enthusiasm in imitating Krsna’s stealing butter and breaking the yogurt pots, Yogamaya played the role of Yasoda and performed the required actions. "O naughty child, you have stolen butter and run away. I will tie you up." Yogamaya, playing the role of a gopi imitating Yasoda, bound up a gopi with a garland. The gopi hid her face with her two hands, enacting fear.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    One gopī acted as Yaśodā as previously described. The other gopī who was slender because of suffering from separation acted as Kṛṣṇa. Another gopī acted as the mortar. The gopī made movements with her eyes to suggest fear (sudṛk). She covered her face with her two hands, acting like a fearful child. She imitated his trembling and crying. They also enacted other pastimes.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Now imitation predominantly mental is described. One gopīs, different from the others, a messenger who was more elderly (anayā), following behind acted as the mother. Or one gopīs who was most gentle, most outstanding acted as his mother. Previously his mother had bound him up with a very soft rope of cow hair. Or first with a garland, and then with another material (anayā) a gopī acting as Kṛṣṇa was bound. Attempting to tie him up many times, they were able to bind him with a garland. They acted according to their fancy. One gopī was thin. Because of the pain of separation she immediately became thin. Out of prema they imitated the Lord being controlled by his devotee. Tatra can mean “in that imitation” or among the gopīs (tatra) one became the mortar. One gopī imitated fear by moving her eyes and covered her face with her hands. This is a quality of a small child when he is afraid. She imitated his characteristics of fear: trembling, hairs standing on end, crying slightly and pitiful voice. By imitating fear, it is imitation of his mentality. Fear is a product of the mind. The Dāmodara pastime, which shows he is controlled by the devotee is the best of all pastimes. Thus it is at the end since one should conclude with sweetness: madhureṇa samāpayet. Since killing Dhenuka and Pralambha were done by Balarāma, they were not enacted. They did not imitate his stealing the gopīs clothing or attracting the wives of the brāhmaṇa, since they were shy. They did not consider the particular rasas of each pastime, since they concluded in the soul of the rasas (Kṛṣṇa) Breaking the Yamalāruna trees was not imitated as it was included in the Dāmodara pastime. The pastimes imitated are not in correct order because Śukadeva, in describing the gopīs bewilderment in separation attained a similar bhāva and gave up inspecting the sequence closely. Or the gopīs imitated the pastimes in the order written, for single to group enactments, and in that, from lesser to major pastimes. Or they manifested the pastimes from single to group enactments. Or because of pain in separation or absorption in the enactments they lost awareness of the correct order.

    Personal Guidance
    Tying a friend with a flower garland echoes Yaśodā binding Kṛṣṇa. Love that binds is sweeter than power that compels — Kṛṣṇa lets Himself be tied by affection alone.
    Reflection Questions
    • What loving 'rope' do I offer Kṛṣṇa that lets Him stay close?
    • Where am I trying to force what only tenderness can hold?
    Analogy

    When the most-beloved story in the household is the time mother tied the boy to the mortar, the children will, decade after decade, re-tie each other with garlands and cower in mock-fear. One gopī binds another with a flower-rope and declares: now I will bind the butter-thief! Vraja's children play Dāmodara at the churn.

    Stories
    Dāmodara-līlā

    Yaśodā tied Kṛṣṇa to the wooden mortar with rope after His butter-theft and broken pot — but every rope was two fingers short of the next, no matter how many she joined, until He accepted being bound (SB 10.9). Hence Dāmodara, 'bound at the belly.'

    The gopī tying her slender friend with a flower-garland and playing the role of Yaśodā the binder is re-enacting Dāmodara-līlā. The second gopī, covering her face in mock-fear, plays Kṛṣṇa Himself — eyes shut, accepting being bound, the world's smallest captive. Sanātana Gosvāmī's Bṛhad-bhāgavatāmṛta treats this as the supreme demonstration that prema binds Bhagavān when nothing else can.
